When accessible voting isn’t accessible: A blind voter’s experience at the polls

by Baylee Alger / Wisconsin Watch, Wisconsin Watch
November 12, 2026

Shortly before the election I wrote about the barriers to voting I face as someone who is blind. I described how, at almost 27 years old, I had never voted because I worried about a lack of privacy in the process. 

Traditional ways of voting would require me to get someone else’s help — whether checking boxes on a paper ballot or choosing a candidate on a screen. 

But while reporting the story, I learned about a machine called the Express Vote, which helps blind and low-vision voters mark ballots electronically, enlarge the print on the screen and use screen readers with headphones. 

I gave it a try on Election Day. Unfortunately, the machine didn’t work. 

Here’s what happened and why it matters. 

Because this was my first time voting, I came prepared, bringing proper documentation. After registering, I asked poll workers for the Express Vote, and they led me over to it. I can only describe it as a large screen, a bit like a giant iPad, set up on a plastic table with a chair in front of it. A set of headphones was plugged into it, and when I put them on, I heard a voice repeating: “To begin accessible voting, press any key on the accessible voting console.”

The trouble? There were no physical keys. Another piece of the machine was missing, too. 

After a while, we realized it wouldn’t work. So I filled out a traditional ballot with help from my mother, who accompanied me to the polls. 

The poll workers apologized profusely. 

I hold no ill will toward them. The equipment is not used often, and staff likely had limited, if any, training on how to operate it. 

But the situation highlights a key point from my original article: Although people with visual disabilities can privately cast their ballots in theory, election workers aren’t always properly equipped or trained to make that happen. 

Still, I’m glad I got to vote, and I think everyone involved learned from this situation. People with disabilities do have options, and that’s what matters most to me.
